list.listitem: The use of electronic fetal monitoring, cesarean delivery, or any other intervention during delivery has not been shown to prevent cerebral palsy (CP) in term infants born to low-risk mothers. A
Magnesium sulfate given to women at risk of preterm birth reduces rates of CP. A

Children suspected of having CP based on developmental delays and an abnormal physical examination should be started in speech, physical, and occupational therapies as early as possible even if a definitive diagnosis has yet to be made and referral considered for assessment using standardized tools. C However, there is little supporting evidence of long-term benefit for physical or surgical therapies.

Recommended standardized tools, in addition to clinical signs and symptoms, for early detection of CP in children 5 months or less are term-age magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), the Prechtl Qualitative Assessment of General Movements, and the Hammersmith Infant Neurological Examination. After 5 months’ corrected age, the most predictive tools for detecting CP risk are MRI, the Hammersmith Infant Neurological Examination, and the Developmental Assessment of Young Children. B

Emotionally supporting the family and the patient and coordinating the patient's care are critical roles for the primary care physician. C Psychosocial interventions are effective in reducing caregiver stress. B
Clonidine and intrathecal baclofen may improve dystonia and clonidine, intrathecal baclofen and botulinum toxin (BtA) may be helpful for improving goal achievement, pain, and ease of caregiving. B

BtA is effective for upper extremity spasticity and is recommended based on a systematic review and evidence-based guideline. A
Low-quality evidence supports use of BtA to improve gait. B
CP is not progressive, but function tends to decline with age. C

background.definition: CP is a disability resulting from damage to the brain before, during, or shortly after birth. Typical manifestations include muscular incoordination and speech disturbances. CP is classified by the main type of movement disorder into four categories: spastic (muscle stiffness), dyskinetic (uncontrollable movements), ataxic (poor balance and coordination), and mixed.

list.listitem: Three per 1000 children aged 5 to 10 years on the basis of Metropolitan Atlanta Developmental Disabilities Surveillance Program Data for 1991 to 1994.

Based on 2008 data from the Autism and Developmental Disabilities Monitoring (ADDM) CP Network, prevalence among 8-year-olds ranges from 2.5/1000 in Missouri to 3.6/1000 in Georgia. CP was more common among boys and among black vs. white or Hispanic children. Most children (77.4%) had spastic CP and over half (58.2%) of children with CP could walk independently.

Risk is higher with greater prematurity. Among children born at 32-28 weeks’ gestation, authors of a meta-analysis of 76 studies found a relative risk of cerebral palsy at 32 to 33 weeks of 14.1 (95% confidence intervals [CI] 12.3-16.0), at 34 to 36 weeks of 3.5 (95% CI 3.2-3.9) and at 37 to 38 weeks, 1.4 (95% CI 1.3-1.6).

Registry data from 19 US academic centers of 10,848 infants born at 22-28 weeks' gestational age from 2013-2018, show 8,495 (78.3%) survived to discharge and, at 2-year follow-up, 8.4% (214/2555) of children had moderate to severe CP. Overall, of fully evaluated children at two years, 48.7% (1198/2458) had no or mild neurodevelopmental impairment, 29.3% (709/2419) had moderate impairment, and 21.2% (512/2419) had severe impairment.

Using registry data from 25 centers of the Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development Neonatal Research Network, of 6927 surviving children born at <27 weeks of gestation and followed at 18 through 26 months of corrected age, 1303 (18.8%) had CP and the remainder had abnormal neurologic examinations not classified as CP.

Children born following assisted reproductive technology have a slightly increased risk of CP compared to those spontaneously conceived (OR 1.3, 95% CI 1.1 to 1.4), but increased risk was demonstrated only among singleton births.
For individuals born with CP in 2000, the estimated lifetime costs in 2003 in dollars were estimated at $11.5 billion. The estimated average lifetime cost for additional care per patient is $921,000.
National Institutes of Health funding for CP research averaged $30 million/year between 2001 and 2013; however, CP in adulthood was the main focus of only 4% of all funding.

In the data registry study of children born at <27 weeks noted above, children with CP were more likely to have multiple medical comorbidities, neurosensory problems, and poor growth at follow-up than those with abnormal neurologic examinations not classified as CP.
Among children in the 2008 ADDM survey with CP, 41% had co-occurring epilepsy and 6.9% had cooccurring autism (vs. 1% in the general population).
Among individuals with CP, the prevalence of drooling, swallowing, and feeding problems is 44.0%, 50.4%, and 53.5%, respectively, based on a systematic review of 42 studies.
In a meta-analysis of 67 studies of children with CP, the estimated prevalence of malnutrition was 40% (95% CI 28.0-53.0).

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 65 articles including 28,429 adults with CP found that most reported fatigue, and a majority experience pain (65.1%; 95% CI, 55.1-74.5), were ambulant (57.9%; 95% CI, 51.1-64.6), and had little or no difficulty with manual ability (65.5%; 95% CI, 61.2-69.7). On average, 40% were employed and 30% lived independently, although these figures were significantly higher for those without intellectual disability at 90% and 72.6%, respectively. The most common comorbidities were epilepsy (28.8%; 95% CI, 20.1-38.4) and asthma (28.3%; 95% CI, 18.7-38.9).

In another systematic review and meta-analysis of 65 papers reporting on chronic health conditions in adults with CP, at least one in five reported depression (21%), anxiety (21%), mood affective disorders (23%), asthma (24%), hypertension (26%, epilepsy (28%), urinary incontinence (32%), malnutrition (38%), and scoliosis (46%). Compared to adults without CP, those with CP were more likely to have type 2 diabetes, anxiety, bipolar disorder, depression, schizophrenia, hypertension, ischemic heart disease, stroke, cerebrovascular disease, asthma, liver disease, osteoarthritis, osteoporosis, underweight, and chronic kidney disease.
Etiology is multifactorial, with known causes accounting for only a small portion of cases.
Prematurity is a factor in an increasing percentage of these patients.
Known causes include hypoxic ischemic encephalopathy, chorioamnionitis, and trauma (e.g., shaken baby).

Authors of a meta-analysis of 38 studies of neurodevelopmental outcomes among preterm infants suffering intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH) or white matter injury (WMI) found higher risks of CP in those with IVH grade 1 to 2 (odds ratio [OR] 1.8, 95% CI 1.4-2.2) or IVH grade 3 to 4 (OR 5, 95% CI 4.1-6.0). Children with WMI had higher risks of CP (OR 14.9, 95% CI 7.3-30.5).
In a meta-analysis of 16 studies with 193 fetuses with intracranial hemorrhage, 32.0% (95% CI, 22.2-42.6%) of the 165 survivors had CP.

Among infants with necrotizing enterocolitis, the incidence of CP was 18% based on 31 studies with 2403 infants. CP was the most common neurodevelopmental impairment (NDI), which occurred in 40% (IQR 28%-64%).

Children exposed to maternal unintentional injury had an increased risk of CP compared to those unexposed (adjusted hazard ratio [HR] 1.3, 95% CI 1.2-1.5) based on a population-based, longitudinal, cohort study of all in-hospital live births in Ontario, Canada (2002 to 2017). Severe injuries resulting in hospitalization and delivery within 1 week from the injury conferred higher risks of CP (adjusted HR 2.2, 95% CI 1.3-3.7 and adjusted HR 3.4, 95% CI 1.9-6.0, respectively).

Congenital cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection was significantly associated with the development of CP in children, with authors of a systematic review of 12 studies finding a pooled prevalence of CP among patients diagnosed with congenital CMV infection of 26% (95% CI 13-40%).

In the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE 2017) guideline for CP in individuals <age 25 years, MRI findings in children with CP include white matter damage (45%), basal ganglia or deep grey matter damage (13%), congenital malformation (10%) and focal infarcts (7%).

Investigators using a longitudinal study examined the relationship between fetal heart rate and type of brain injury on MRI in 140 preterm infants with severe CP. CP was presumed to have an antenatal onset in 57% of infants and to have been caused by an intrapartum insult in 13% of infants. MRI findings in 34% (n=48) of infants showed basal ganglia-thalamus-dominant brain injury which was associated with continuous bradycardia and persistently non-reassuring fetal heart rate patterns, although confidence intervals were wide. Of the remaining 92 infants, 43% (60) showed white matter injuries, 1% (1) showed watershed injuries, 4% (5) showed stroke, 1% (1) had normal findings, and 18% (25) had unclassified findings.

Exome sequencing is a genomic technique for sequencing the protein-coding regions of genes in a genome which comprise about 1% of the genome, but about 80% of all expressed genes. Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 13 studies performing exome or genome sequencing on 2612 individuals with CP found a diagnostic yield of 31.1% (95% CI, 24.2%-38.6%; I2 = 91%).

In another study, genetic causes of CP were investigated comparing the diagnostic yield in 15 study cohorts with 2419 individuals using exome sequencing and 5 studies with 294 individuals using copy number variants assessed by chromosomal microarray (CMA). The diagnostic yield of exome sequencing across cases with no known CP risk factors (cryptogenic CP cohorts) was 35% (95% CI, 27%-45%) compared with 7% (95% CI, 4%-12%) across cohorts with known risk factors. The diagnostic yield of CMA was 5% (95% CI, 2%-12%).
Injury to the developing fetal brain or immature brain at or around birth.

The location of injury will determine symptoms: Spasticity occurs when descending tracts that inhibit the reflex arc are injured, causing uncontrolled facilitation and muscle contraction. If the basal ganglia are injured, posture and automatic movements can be affected. Injuries to the cerebellum can cause hypotonia, problems with proprioception, balance problems, and tremors.

In very preterm neonates, white matter injury in frontal, parietal, and temporal lobes are associated with adverse motor outcomes, but only frontal white front matter volumes predicted adverse cognitive outcomes.

list.listitem: There are no recommended standard screening procedures for CP. C

At well child visits, look for early indicators of CP: failure to meet gross and fine motor developmental milestones, abnormal muscle tone or deep tendon reflexes, persistence of primitive reflexes, delayed development of normal postural reflexes. C

Based on a single RCT of 548 women carrying preterm fetuses with suspected in utero compromise, immediate delivery vs. expectant management did not reduce perinatal morbidity or mortality; in fact, more children in the immediate delivery group had CP at or after 2 years of age (RR 5.88; 95% CI, 1.33-26.02) although there were no differences in neurodevelopment impairment at or after 2 years of age (RR 1.72; 95% CI, 0.86-3.41).

Magnesium sulfate given to women at risk of preterm birth reduces rates of CP. A Based on limited evidence, magnesium may be most effective when administered to patients in preterm labor at <32 weeks’ gestation and antenatal corticosteroids are most effective for those who deliver within 7 days. B

Authors of an overview of Cochrane reviews and an individual participant data meta-analysis on antenatal interventions to prevent CP found high-quality evidence that antenatal magnesium sulfate (MgSO4) for women at risk of preterm birth reduced rates of CP (RR 0.68; 95% CI, 0.54-0.87; number needed to treat = 48) . Potentially harmful interventions from single trials were prophylactic antibiotics for preterm labor (RR 1.82; 95% CI, 0.99-3.34) and immediate vs. delayed delivery of preterm infants with suspected fetal compromise (RR 5.88; 95% CI, 1.33-26.02). Repeated doses of corticosteroids for women at risk of preterm birth are probably ineffective and there is insufficient evidence to assess benefits for antenatal corticosteroids, magnesium sulfate or interventionist care for pre-eclampsia, prenatal progesterone or betamimetics for preventing preterm birth.

In an RCT of 560 pregnant women at risk for preterm delivery before 32 weeks of gestation, crude rates of moderate to severe CP were decreased in the MgSO4 group given a 5 g loading dose followed by 1 g/hour compared to the placebo group (2.0% and 3.3%, respectively; adjusted OR 0.61; 95% CI 0.23-1.65).

In a large RCT of women at high risk of preterm delivery, MgSO4 was effective in reducing rates of CP compared to placebo among the 1979 infants evaluated at age 2 years (4.2% vs. 6.9%; OR 0.59; 95% CI, 0.39-0.88). This reduction was partially explained by a decreased risk of developing intracerebral echodensities and echolucencies in children delivered at <32 weeks gestation. Exposure to MgSO4 does not appear to affect neonatal resuscitation or other short-term outcomes. There is no clear difference in perinatal death based on randomized trials comparing antenatal MgSO4 with placebo/no treatment.

In an RCT of 1433 pregnant individuals expected to deliver at 30 to 34 weeks’ gestation, antenatal administration of magnesium sulfate (4 g) did not result in differences in death or CP at 2 years' corrected age between the magnesium and placebo groups (3.3% vs 2.7% for placebo). Neonates in the magnesium group were less likely to have respiratory distress syndrome vs. the placebo group (34% vs 41%, respectively) and chronic lung disease (5.6% vs. 8.2%, respectively).

Authors of a meta-analysis of 6 RCTs with 6037 infants comparing intravenous MgSO4 of varying doses (4 grams to 6 grams followed by maintenance doses of 0 to 3 grams per hour) with placebo given prior to preterm birth found reduced risk for CP in children born preterm (3.4% vs. 5.0%; RR 0.68, 95% CI, 0.54-0.85) across a wide range of gestational ages without documented adverse effects.
Exposure to magnesium <12 hours before delivery is associated with a reduction in CP compared with more remote exposure (2.3% vs. 4.4%; adjusted OR 0.41; 95% CI, 0.18-0.91).

In a secondary analysis of a national population-based cohort (France) of 2613 preterm neonates who received antenatal corticosteroids, overall survival was 96.6% and survival without moderate or severe neurologic disabilities was 86% (95% CI 84.7-87.0). Administration of steroids 7 or more days prior to birth was associated with lower rates of survival without moderate or severe neurologic disabilities (85%) compared with receiving steroids from day 3 to day 7 (87%) (adjusted OR 0.70; 95% CI 0.54-0.89).

Neither hydrocortisone given for 7 days following birth nor prophylactic early high-dose recombinant human erythropoietin were effective for preventing CP or improving neurodevelopmental impairment at 2 years in extremely preterm infants.

Among infants with birth weights <1000 g, a strategy of liberal blood transfusions vs. restrictive transfusions did not reduce the likelihood of death or disability, including CP (4.3% vs. 5.6%, respectively) at 24 months of corrected age.
Similarly, use of an initial lower (0.3) or higher (0.6-0.65) FiO2 during stabilization of extremely preterm infants does not influence rates of CP or neurodevelopmental outcomes at age 2 years.
Therapeutic hypothermia may be effective at reducing mortality and disability in infants with hypoxic ischemic encephalopathy.

The National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence (NICE 2012; revisited 2016) suggests offering a hip X-ray to children with bilateral cerebral palsy at 24 months of age. Consider hip X-rays annually in children or young people who are at Gross Motor Function Classification System (GMFCS) level III, IV, or V or after 6 months in children and young people where the initial hip migration is greater than 30%, and then consider repeating the hip X-ray every 6 months after this if the hip migration is increasing by more than 10 percentage points per year.

As chronic health conditions appear earlier among adults with CP, consider routine screening for hearing loss, aspiration, osteoporosis (especially among those on anti-epileptic medications), pain, mental health disorders, sleep disorders, urinary incontinence, and decubitus ulcers among those who are non-ambulatory.
Take a thorough history including the mother's prenatal course, labor and delivery, and a history of the child's development. C
A physical examination revealing abnormal muscle tone in a child with failure to reach developmental motor milestones should raise the index of suspicion. C
Selective use of neuroimaging (MRI), EEG, and metabolic and genetic testing is recommended if the etiology is unclear or if the patient has features suggestive of seizure or other syndrome. C

Complete neurologic assessment should be included in all well child visits to look for early indicators of CP such as failure to meet gross and fine motor developmental milestones, abnormal muscle tone (stiffness or tightness in the legs between 6 and 12 months* such as inability to bring the toes to mouth) or abnormal deep tendon reflexes, persistence of primitive reflexes (e.g., fisting of hands past 4 months*), or delayed development of normal postural reflexes. Additional signs suggestive of CP, based on expert consensus, are asymmetry in posture or movement after 4 months* and early hand preference before 12 months of age*.
History should include mother's pregnancy, labor, and delivery.

Developmental history should include achievement of milestones and delay in achievement of gross motor skills such as persistent head lag beyond 4 months* or delayed sitting without support beyond 9 months*, and delayed crawling and walking.
Such delay, combined with abnormal muscle tone, deep tendon reflexes, postural reflexes, and/or primitive reflexes, suggests the diagnosis of CP.

In one study, consistent assessment using the 6 starred signs and symptoms above led to significantly earlier diagnosis of CP from a weighted average of 19.5 months (95% CI, 16.2-22.8) to 9.5 months (95% CI, 4.5-14.6).
Children with CP should be screened for mental retardation, ophthalmologic and hearing impairments, and speech and language disorders.

Authors of a systematic review with 2908 children with CP found a high prevalence of sleep disorders, with a pooled prevalence of 26.9% (95% CI, 21.5%-32.7%) for disorders of initiation and maintenance of sleep - the most prevalent sleep problem reported.

Pain should be assessed in children with spastic CP (see complications below). In a prospective database of 331 children/adolescents with lower limb and 155 with upper limb spasticity from three phase 3 trials, spasticity-related pain with at least one activity was self-reported in 81.9% and 69.7%, respectively at baseline. Pain negatively affected the great majority in many ways.

Adults with CP should be screened for hearing loss, aspiration, osteoporosis, pain, mental health disorders, sleep disorders, urinary incontinence, and decubitus ulcers (if non-ambulatory). NICE (2019) recommends consideration of dual-energy X ray absorptiometry assessment in adults with CP who have 2 or more risk factors (needing help with moving, history of falls, low BMI, history of low-impact fractures, or other medical factors such as steroid use, that may adversely affect bone health).Monitor for common problems including constipation, acid reflux, seizures, worsening spasticity, muscle contractures, and malnutrition.

Severity can be assessed by using the Gross Motor Function Classification System (). Upper extremity function can be assessed with the Manual Ability Classification System and the Communication Function Classification System can be used for assessing communication proficiency.
While these classification systems are geared towards children with CP, they can be used for adults.

The World Health Organization International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health contains health and health-related domains and can be used to measure health and disability at both individual and population levels.

For assessment of dysphagia in children with CP, the Schedule for Oral Motor Assessment and the Functional Feeding Assessment, modified, appear to have best psychometric properties while the former and the Dysphagia Disorders Survey were found in this review to have the strongest clinical utility.
Drooling can be assessed using the 5-minute drooling quotient (DQ) that performed as well as the 10-minute DQ; assessment was most accurate when the child was active (vs. at rest).
There are no imaging or laboratory studies that are diagnostic for CP.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 4 studies concluded that for children born at term, acidosis measured with umbilical cord pH was not significantly associated with CP at 1 year (RR 3.4, 95% CI 0.9-13.3).
MRI imaging is recommended (preferably MRI) when the etiology of CP has not been established.

Recommended standardized tools, in addition to clinical signs and symptoms, for early detection of CP are term-age MRI (86%-89% sensitivity), the Prechtl Qualitative Assessment of General Movements (98% sensitivity), and the Hammersmith Infant Neurological Examination (90% sensitivity). After 5 months’ corrected age, the most predictive tools for detecting risk are MRI (86%-89% sensitivity), the Hammersmith Infant Neurological Examination (90% sensitivity), and the Developmental Assessment of Young Children (83% C index).

Metabolic and genetic studies are not routinely recommended but should be considered if the etiology remains unclear after a careful history and neuroimaging or if specific patient features suggest a genetic or metabolic problem (such as brain malformation).
Consider an evaluation for coagulation disorder in patients with hemiplegic CP with an unexplained cerebral infarction.
An EEG should only be obtained when the child or adult with CP has symptoms of seizure disorder.

Authors of a case-control study developed a prognostic tool to apply to term neonates for identification of those at increased risk of developing CP. The factors included in the final model were tobacco or drug use, diabetes, preeclampsia, chorioamnionitis, prolonged rupture of membranes, male sex), number of pregnancies, number of miscarriages, 5-minute Apgar score, infant weight (and a weight2 term), and gestational age in weeks. The model correctly classified 75% of infants with a sensitivity of 56%, specificity of 82% and C statistic of 0.74 (95% CI 71-76).

Evaluation begins with clinical suspicion based on history (e.g., preterm birth, encephalopathy, intra-uterine growth retardation), parental concern, and delayed gross motor milestones or findings of abnormal muscle tone on physical examination.

An expert panel noted two warning signs that would prompt monitoring rather than referral for CP diagnosis – persistent startle (Moro) reflex beyond 6 months of age and consistent toe-walking or asymmetric walking beyond 12 months of age.

Use experienced pediatric physical, occupational, and speech therapists to evaluate the child with suspected CP. Standardized tools such as the Prechtl Qualitative Assessment of General Movements, the Hammersmith Infant Neurological Examination and the Developmental Assessment of Young Children should be part of the assessment.
Referral to a developmental pediatrician or pediatric neurologist, if they are available, is helpful to confirm the diagnosis and guide therapeutic interventions.
The NICE (2017 and 2019) guidelines also note that access to providers of orthotics, orthopedic surgery, and/or neurosurgery may be needed and provided locally or regionally.

Guidelines from an international panel of experts recommend that interventions targeting function include client-chosen goals, whole-task practice within real-life settings, support to empower families, and a team approach.

Caregivers report many challenges in caring for and raising a child with CP including need for convenient healthcare facilities, therapeutic services, and accessible public places; need for healthcare information and financial aid; psychological and physical constraints; societal rejection and stigma; and an overwhelming caring burden. Healthcare providers should solicit concerns and help prepare and support caregivers.
Early institution of speech, physical, and occupational therapy is the widely accepted first-line treatment; such therapy is also a mainstay of care. C

Timing of more invasive therapies and surgery are based on individual patient needs; decisions regarding these interventions should be made in conjunction with parents, therapist(s), and specialist(s) involved in the patient's ongoing care. C

Coordinating the use of specialist and therapeutic modalities to maximize the patient's function and quality of life, and to prevent or treat complications is the ultimate role of the primary care physician. C
Offer information on parent and patient organizations that can provide support, counseling, information, and advocacy. C

Clonidine, intrathecal baclofen and botulinum toxin A (BtA) can be used to improve goal achievement, pain, and ease of caregiving. B Diazepam or enteral (oral or via feeding tube) baclofen can be used if spasticity is contributing to pain, muscle spasm or functional disability; the latter if a long-term effect is desired. B

BtA is effective for upper extremity spasticity and is recommended, in combination with occupational therapy. A
There is limited evidence that BtA is effective for lower limb spasms and improving gait. B
Drug therapy is used to manage spasticity and dystonia and should focus on personal treatment goals, attempting to balance benefits and risks.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 4 RCTs and 42 non-randomized studies found very low-certainty evidence supporting clonidine and intrathecal baclofen to improve dystonia and low to very-low-certainty evidence supporting clonidine, intrathecal baclofen and botulinum toxin for improving goal achievement, pain, and ease of caregiving. All medications were associated with increased adverse events.

Use of BtA intramuscular injections to reduce muscle tone in the upper extremities of children with spastic CP has become a common intervention. A systematic review of 10 RCTs supports the efficacy of BtA in combination with a program of occupational therapy. There is moderate-strength evidence that BtA without therapy is much less effective. Concentrations of BtA ranged from 50 to 200 U/mL and doses from 0.5 to 16 U/kg.

There is no strong evidence to support BtA's effectiveness when used in the lower extremities. However, authors of a Cochrane review of 31 low-quality RCTs including 1508 children with CP found BtA to be more effective than placebo for improving gait, joint range of motion, satisfaction, and lower limb spasticity; results for function were conflicting. Similarly, authors of a meta-analysis of 15 RCTs concluded that BtA and casting contributed to gait improvement in children with CP and spastic equinus foot. BtA was more effective than orthotics in treating ankle contractures but not superior to ankle serial casting.

In a case series of 486 children/adolescents with CP and spasticity-related pain, pain related to difficult activities/tasks was evaluated 4 weeks after each of four incobotulinum toxinA injections. By week 4 of the last (fourth) injection, 33.8% to 53.3% of subjects reported complete pain relief from their baseline pain

Authors of a review of Bt-A caution that majority of clinical trials report fairly short-term outcomes (3-6 months), focus on a single injection cycle, and less often report activity or participation. In addition, muscle atrophy has been reported for at least 12 months following injection accompanied by loss of contractile elements in muscle and replacement with fat and connective tissue that may not be reversible.

In a 10-year follow-up study of 46 children with bilateral spastic CP who participated in an RCT, early treatment with BoNT-A and hip abduction bracing vs. usual care did not reduce the need for surgery or improve hip development at skeletal maturity. BtA, however, is endorsed by evidence-based guidelines from the AAN and NICE.

NICE cautions against use of BtA in patients with severe muscle weakness, those who have had a previous adverse reaction or allergy to BtA or who are receiving aminoglycoside treatment. Also use caution for children or young people with bleeding disorders, generalized spasticity, fixed muscle contractures and marked bony deformity. Serious side effects of BtA include swallowing and breathing difficulties.

For treatment of drooling, data from 6 trials were insufficient to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of BtA or the pharmaceutical interventions benztropine and glycopyrrolate. A larger meta-analysis (16 trials) found temporary benefit from salivary-gland BtA injections, with pooled results showing reduced drooling frequency and one RCT reporting an almost 30% reduction in the impact of drooling on patients' lives.

Based on a single-center pediatric saliva control cohort of 483 children, the greatest improvement in drooling was seen after intraglandular BtA injections (n = 207, 551 courses, mean Drooling Impact Scale (DIS) score change 34.7) or duct transpositional surgery (n = 31, mean change in DIS 29.0). Oral anticholinergics glycopyrronium bromide and trihexyphenidyl were associated with good outcomes (n = 237, mean change in DIS 21.5 and 22.4, respectively).

Diazepam is probably effective and tizanidine is possibly effective in reducing spasticity, but both have uncertain effects on motor function and carry adverse effects. ANN found insufficient data to support or refute the use of dantrolene, oral baclofen, continuous intrathecal baclofen, phenol, or alcohol. NICE (2019) recommends diazepam only in acute situations when spasticity is causing severe pain or anxiety.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 19 studies found intrathecal baclofen had a significant effect on the reduction of spasticity (SMD for spasticity reduction - 1.7 (95% CI - 2.2 to -1.2) in patients with CP. They also noted a small but statistically significant improvement in motor function. Among 501 intrathecal baclofen implantations, 203 medical complications were reported including six new-onset seizures (3% of medical complications), seven increased seizure frequency (3.4%), 33 infections (16.3%), eight meningitis (3.9%), and 16 cerebrospinal fluid leaks (7.9%).

NICE (2019) recommends diazepam or enteral (oral or via feeding tube) baclofen if spasticity is contributing to pain, muscle spasm or functional disability; the latter if a long-term effect is desired. Start with a low dose and increase gradually over 4 weeks.

NICE also recommends consideration of continuous pump-administered intrathecal baclofen in patients who failed non-invasive therapy and have spasticity or dystonia causing pain, muscle spasms or difficulty with posture, function or self-care. In an RCT of 33 patients with severe dyskinetic CP in the Netherlands, intrathecal baclofen was superior to placebo in goal attainment scaling of individual treatment goals at 3 months, with similar adverse effects reported between groups.

In a double‐blind, cross‐over trial in 16 children with predominant dystonic CP, there was no difference in mean follow‐up scores for change in dystonia, upper limb function, or improved activities of daily living in those randomized to trihexyphenidyl, an antispasmotic, antimuscarinic agent, vs. placebo.

Surgical treatment of thumb-in-palm deformity can help with hygiene, appearance, and quality of life. However, surgical approaches are not standardized, and no high-quality study of the available techniques has been performed.

Authors of a recent meta-analysis of 73 small cohort studies and one small RCT examining the effectiveness of multilevel surgery for children with spastic CP found no benefit on long-term gross motor function (standardized mean difference [SMD]: 0.38; 95% confidence interval [CI], -0.25 to 1.01) or gait speed (SMD: 0.12; 95% CI, -0.01 to 0.25) but there was evidence of improved gait (SMD: -0.80; 95% CI, -0.95 to -0.65). Few studies examined participation or quality of life.

NICE recommends consideration of orthopedic referral for children and young people with hip migration >30% or increasing by >10 percentage points per year; limited limb function; contractures of the shoulder, elbow, wrist, or hand that cause difficulty with skin hygiene; or for poor cosmetic appearance of the upper limb that causes significant concern to the patient and family.

In a follow-up study 163 patients (mean age 14 years) with spastic non-ambulatory CP who underwent triradiate cartilage closure, 22.1% had an unsuccessful hip outcome. Independent risk factors for an unsuccessful hip outcome were first hip migration percentage ≥35% and pelvic obliquity.

Selective dorsal rhizotomy has been reported in a small case series to be moderately effective for children with spastic hemiparesis. NICE recommends consideration of its use to improve walking ability in children and young people with spasticity at GMFCS level II or III. NICE (2019) suggests consideration of selective dorsal rhizotomy for adults with cerebral palsy and spasticity if other treatments have failed or are contraindicated, and after assessment by a multidisciplinary team. Patients and their families should understand that the procedure is irreversible and long-term outcomes are uncertain.

In a 9-year follow-up study of children undergoing distal rectus femoris transfer for correction of stiff-knee gait in spastic diplegic CP, corrective surgery appeared effective in improving peak knee flexion, especially for those with the most involvement, but 18% showed a permanently poor response and 15% developed recurrence. When this procedure was performed prophylactically, there was no apparent benefit. Functional outcomes were not reported.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 14 studies of rectus femoris transfer for stiff knee gait in patients with CP and 5 studies of distal RF release transfer found that only transfer improved Peak Knee Flexion in swing phase, with a small effect size (SMD=0.3).

In one study of 39 children (29 randomized) with upper-extremity CP who were candidates for standard tendon transfer, surgical treatment provided greater improvement in movement and satisfaction than BtA injections or regular, ongoing therapy at 12-month follow-up. Pinch strength was greater in both the surgical and therapy groups than BtA injections.

Authors of a systematic review of traditional Chinese remedies identified 35 RCTs involving 3286 children with CP of low methodologic quality. They provided limited support for acupuncture and combinations of acupuncture with herbal medicine or conventional therapy.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 15 RCTs on acupuncture for improving dystonia in children with CP concluded that acupuncture combined with routine treatment was more effective than routine treatment alone for reducing muscle tension.

Early institution of speech, physical, and occupational therapy is the widely accepted first-line in treatment; such therapy is also a mainstay of care. Authors of a Cochrane review found positive trends in communication change with speech and language therapy but study quality was poor and skill maintenance was not thoroughly assessed.

Parent-delivered multidomain early intervention for infants with CP compared to health advice controls resulted in no overall effect at 18 months, but superior improvements in motor skills in ambulant children.

To improve walking ability, the consensus international guidelines recommend overground walking supplemented with treadmill training.Backward walking training also appears to be as effective or slightly superior to forward walking training for improving walking speed in children with CP based on a meta-analysis.

International guidelines recommend approaches that can facilitate hand use goals include bimanual therapy, constraint-induced movement therapy, goal-directed training, and cognitive approaches. For self-care, they recommend whole-task practice combined with assistive devices and participation in leisure goals that combine whole-task practice with strategies to address environmental, personal, and social barriers.

In an RCT comparing 2 weeks (50 hours) of hand-arm bimanual intensive therapy vs. usual motor activity including 50 children with unilateral CP, mean age 35.3 months, intensive therapy resulted in improved motor performance at 3 months compared to controls.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 27 RCT, including 847 participants with spastic CP, found positive effects from strength training programs compared to other physical therapy techniques or untreated control groups for knee flexor, extensor and plantarflexor muscle strength; maximum resistance; balance; gait speed; gross motor function and spasticity.

Authors of a Cochrane review found that treadmill intervention may improve gross motor skill attainment in children with cerebral palsy, but data are limited. In an RCT of 19 children aged 14 to 32 months with spastic diplegic CP, there were no differences in gross motor function measures, walking attainment or overall walking activity between children randomized to 6 weeks of twice weekly vs. 10 times weekly treadmill training.
NICE recommends an adapted physical therapy program following procedures such BtA, continuous pump-administered intrathecal baclofen, orthopedic surgery, or selective dorsal rhizotomy.

Authors of a Cochrane review of exercise (aerobic, resistance or mixed training) in patients with CP found many small trials at high risk of bias. The authors concluded that for children, aerobic exercise may improve gross motor function but not gait speed and resistance training conferred no apparent benefit.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 15 RCTs including 414 participants with CP concluded that aerobic exercise improves gross motor function, mobility, aerobic capacity, balance and participation. It does not improve gait parameters, quality of life, muscle strength or spasticity.

For children with CP and pulmonary dysfunction, various types of physical therapy including inspiratory muscle training, aerobic training, swimming, respiratory exercise, and exercise with elastic bands have a positive effect on maximal inspiratory pressure, peak expiratory flow and oxygen consumption.

Respiratory therapy resulted in improved inspiratory muscle strength and pulmonary function (0.60, 95%CI 0.38-0.82, n = 98) based on a meta-analysis of 10 studies including 324 children with CP. Functional skills in daily living activities also improved in the intervention group.

Robotic gait training was also found to be of benefit on gait speed, endurance, and gross motor function in a systematic review of 10 trials. However, in a meta-analysis of 8 RCTs examining robotic gait training alone compared to standard gait training in individuals with CP, there was no difference in walk test performance, free walking speed or Gross Motor Function Measures.
The addition of robotic training to treadmill walking to facilitate weight-shift and leg swing improved walking speed and 6-minute walking distance in one small RCT.

NICE recommends 24-hour postural management strategies such as low-load active stretching or low-load passive stretching to prevent or delay the development of contractures or skeletal deformities in children and young people at risk of developing these and to enable the patient to participate in appropriate activities.
NICE also recommends consideration of constraint-induced movement therapy followed by bimanual therapy (unrestrained use of both arms) to enhance manual skills.

Two small RCTs for spastic unilateral CP, showed improved motor gains (2004) and improved functional performance and health-related quality of life (2012) with constraint-induced therapy (restraint of the unaffected limb and intensive use of the affected limb) vs. traditional rehabilitation.

Authors of a Cochrane review of 36 trials with 1264 children ranging from three months to 19.8 years found low-quality evidence that constraint-induced therapy resulted in improved bimanual performance and unimanual capacity compared to a low-dose comparison such as occupational therapy but not when compared to high-dose (e.g., individual occupational therapy or bimanual therapy) or dose-matched therapies.

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 12 RCTs and 3 non-controlled clinical trials found some benefit of resistance therapy intervention on motor function, with an SMD of 0.37, 95% CI, 0.21-0.52, although there was high heterogeneity across studies.

There was no significant benefit of a 16-week stretching and progressive resistance exercise program followed by a 16-week maintenance program on muscle strength in a small RCT of children with spastic bilateral CP.

Neurodevelopmental therapy (NDT), characterized by hands-on “therapist-guided” facilitation of movement to provide sensory input and improve postural control, had no effect compared to control therapy for improving motor function. These authors also found a moderate effect favoring activity-based approaches over NDT.

Conflicting evidence was reported among 9 RCTs examining on-the-ground activity for children with CP with the meta-analysis of trials showing no benefit compared to no intervention on improving activity or participation.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 9 studies of cycling interventions with 282 children with CP found a nonsignificant improvement in gross motor function (SMD 0.35, 95% CI, -0.01 to 0.70); the effect was clearly insignificant when one poor-quality study was omitted.

Virtual reality games may help improve gross motor skills in children with CP based on a meta-analysis of 7 RCTs with 234 children with CP, with an SMD of 0.37, 95% CI, 0.06-0.68. In a larger meta-analysis of 17 RCTs with 853 children, virtual motor training had significant positive effects on activities of daily living, grip strength and gross motor function. Authors of another meta-analysis of 16 RCTs found virtual reality intervention were beneficial for balance (SMD 0.5, 95% CI 0.3-0.7) for children with CP.

Hippotherapy and therapeutic horseback riding (also known as equine-assisted therapy which focuses on promoting physical and mental health) have a positive effect on lower-limb muscle spasticity in children with CP based on a meta-analysis of 7 studies. Repeated treatment sessions, however, did not show benefit over a single session. In another meta-analysis, authors found strong evidence for a positive effect of equine-assisted therapies, particularly hippotherapy, on global gross motor function and motor capabilities during walking in children with CP, but no effect on quality of life.

Authors of a systematic review found level II evidence supporting therapeutic horse-riding on posture and for neurodevelopmental treatment and functional training on gross motor function in children with CP.

Combination physical therapy with hippotherapy was not more effective than physical therapy alone on gross motor function of children and adolescents with CP based on a meta-analysis of 6 studies with 315 individuals.

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis failed to find conclusive evidence of benefit of use of mechanical horse-riding simulators on sitting postural balance in patients with CP. The simulator may help with adductor spasticity based on an RCT of 24 children with spastic CP.

A 9-week narrative-based educational program to train self-regulated competences and executive function skills administered to 15 children with CP was effective in promoting school engagement in the post-test analysis.

Caregiver stress can be ameliorated by psychosocial interventions. Authors of a systematic review of 13 studies and meta-analysis of 7 studies with 662 participants showed that psychosocial interventions significantly improved parental wellbeing (SMD -0.61, 95% CI, -0.92 to -0.30).
While some children who have difficulty feeding orally may be candidates for placement of a gastrostomy or jejunostomy tube, their use has not been studied in clinical trials.

Use of speech and language therapy for patients with CP is widely used to aid in communication skills. Various types of augmentative and alternative communication interventions tailored to a patient’s needs can be effective in improving receptive and expressive communication skills in patients with CP.

NICE (2017) recommends consideration of orthoses for children and young people with upper limb spasticity to include elbow gaiters to maintain extension and improve function, rigid wrist orthoses to prevent contractures and limit wrist and hand flexion deformity, dynamic orthoses to improve hand function, and ankle–foot orthoses for children and young people with serious functional limitations to improve foot position for sitting, transfers between sitting and standing, and assisted standing. The latter may not be useful for children and young people with secondary complications of spasticity such as contractures and abnormal torsion. They also recommend orthoses following BtA to enhance stretching of the temporarily weakened muscle and improve functional skills.

Functional electrical stimulation was somewhat successful in improving gait and reducing energy expenditure compared with conventional physical therapy over 3 months in a small RCT of children with hemiplegic CP.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 6 low-quality RCTs with 174 patients concluded that neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES) used as an adjuvant therapy improved sitting and standing gross motor function in children with spastic CP but not walking gross motor function. However, in another meta-analysis of 9 studies, functional electrical stimulation increased walking speed of children with CP, and in a meta-analysis of 19 RCTs (including 265 patients with CP in intervention groups and 263 patients with CP in control groups) there was improvement in gross motor function, walking speed, step length, and daily living activities in the intervention group.

Based on a systematic review of 18 studies of 595 children with chronic neuromuscular disorders, including CP, the pooled effect of NMES on gross motor functional measure had a standardized mean difference of 0.41, 95% CI 0.19-0.64.
Whole-body vibration was an effective intervention for improving balance and gait in patients with CP based on a systematic review and meta-analysis of 16 studies.
Deep brain stimulation has some supporting evidence from case reports for treating severe and painful mobile (variable tone) dystonia in adults and children.

Hyperbaric oxygen treatment improved outcomes including gross motor functions (Gross Motor Function Measure SMD 0.29, 95% CI 0.07-0.51, n = 696), global developmental level (Gesell RR 1.30, 95% CI 1.19-1.42, n = 560), language expression (MD 4.34, 95% CI 2.30-6.38, n = 270) and comprehension (MD 4.87, 95% CI 2.87-6.88, n = 270,) based on low-quality evidence from a meta-analysis of 25 studies with 2,146 patients. The primary reported adverse effect was mild ear pain.
Stem cell therapy appears to result in significant improvement in gross motor function in patients with CP (SMD of GMF-66 score [after-before] treatment 1.5 (95% CI 0.7-2.3), I2 89.9%).
Referral to a developmental pediatrician or pediatric neurologist to confirm the diagnosis is appropriate at any point when the diagnosis is suspected.

Seizures occur in approximately one third of children with CP. In a longitudinal cohort study of 256 children with CP, 93 (36%) had one or more febrile or afebrile seizures beyond the neonatal period and 87 (34%) had epilepsy. Fifty-six (60%) of the children with seizures had electroclinical features of a self-limited focal epilepsy of childhood, 28 were diagnosed with focal epilepsy-not otherwise specified, infantile spasms syndrome in 11, Lennox-Gastaut syndrome in three, genetic generalized epilepsies in two and febrile seizures in nine. Favorable seizure outcomes were noted in those with self-limited focal epilepsy-variant with 42/56 (75%) not having a seizure for >2 years. Favorable seizure outcomes were also seen in some children with infantile spasms syndrome and focal epilepsy-not otherwise specified. Of the 93 children with seizures, at last follow-up (mean age 15 years), 61/91 (67%) had not had a seizure in >2 years.

Authors of a systematic review found that among children with CP, 75% were in pain; half had an intellectual disability; one third could not walk; one third had a hip displacement; 1 in 4 had the following problems: inability to talk, epilepsy, behavior disorder, bladder control problems; 1 in 5 had a sleep disorder or had dribbling; 1 in 10 were blind; 1 in 15 required tube-feedings; and 1 in 25 were deaf. Hip displacement was reported in 26% of 335 children with CP in Norway (22% with subluxation and 4% with dislocation) with highest rates (63%) in those with the poorest Gross Motor Function Classification System classes (IV and V).

In a more recent meta-analysis, authors found spasticity-related pain with at least one activity at baseline was self-reported in 81.9% /69.7% (lower/upper limb) of children/adolescents with CP and spasticity.
Tooth grinding is common among children and adolescents with neurodevelopmental disorders, with a prevalence among those with CP of 71.9% (95% CI 52.4-91.4).
Use of bisphosphonates can improve bone mineral density in children with CP and osteoporosis, but there is no direct evidence on reducing fractures.

Pain is common among adults with CP. In a mail survey of 406 adults with CP without intellectual disability in Norway, 82% reported musculoskeletal pain from at least 1 body site. Twenty-eight percent reported daily pain for at least 1 year compared to 15% in a reference group. Mean age of pain onset was 21 years. Back pain was the most common site in most forms of CP. Pain was associated with female gender, chronic fatigue, low life satisfaction and loss of physical function.

Musculoskeletal problems including cervical, back and weight-bearing joint pain and dysfunction were found in 76% of 101 adult patients with moderate-severe CP; these problems developed before age 50 years in 63% of cases.

Participation in sports can improve gait, muscle strength, and functional abilities; however, in patients with CP, ambulant athletes are at risk for soft-tissue injuries in the knee as well as foot and ankle injuries; wheelchair athletes are at risk for osteoporotic fractures and shoulder girdle injuries; and limb-deficient athletes are prone to low back pain and overuse injuries of the contralateral extremity.

Hypertension is common in patients with CP as demonstrated in a systematic review and meta-analysis of 11 international cohorts representing 444 adults with CP; the overall prevalence of hypertension was 28.7% (95% CI 18.8-39.8%).

In a survey of 63 adult women with CP living in the community, aged 20-74 years, pain was the most common problem (84%), followed by hip and back deformity (59%), bowel (56%) and bladder problems (49%), poor dental health (43%), seizures (40%), and GERD (28%).
Higher rates of anxiety and depression for those with CP have also been reported.

In an Australian study of 3507 individuals with CP born between 1970 and 2004, crude mortality was 20% at the age of 40 years. Mortality was highest in children <15 years and decreased to twice the population rate at age 35 years. No independent ambulation was the strongest independent predictor of mortality (adjusted hazard ratio 6.2; 95% CI, 3.3-11.8).

In a UK study of 193 males and 148 females with CP, if surviving to age 20 years, almost 85% of the cohort survived to age 50 years. Diseases of the respiratory system were more common in those dying in their 20s and 30s than in the general population while there were fewer deaths due injuries and accidents. For those people dying in their 40s and 50s, more deaths were attributed to circulatory system and nervous system disease and neoplasms was observed.
Among children with severe CP, about half survive to age 13 years and 25% to age 30 years.
The Gross Motor Function Classification System for CP can be used to reasonably predict the ultimate gross motor function of a child with CP. C
A survey of 129 youths and 70 adults with CP (35% mild, 19% moderate, 47% severe) found significant impairments in self-rated measures of quality of life and health. B

Many adults with CP report deterioration of function with aging, especially for ambulation. Thirty-five percent of adults with CP in a sheltered workshop reported functional deterioration. In a longitudinal study of 72 patients with CP followed into adulthood, while 41% were able to walk independently before age 18 years, only 22% walked independently after age 18 years; of those who were still ambulatory, walking distance declined. In another retrospective survey of 216 persons with CP and no intellectual disability, 10% had lost their walking skills and 44% reported deterioration, mainly before age 35 years. In a chart review study of 30 patients with CP in a special needs clinic, four significant functional losses were identified: crawling, standing independently, walking function, and eating independently.

In a review of nine case-control studies, three components of health-related physical fitness were reduced in young adults with CP vs. controls—muscular strength, muscular endurance, and cardiorespiratory endurance.
NICE (2017) recommends that children be monitored for treatment response, worsening spasticity and secondary consequences of spasticity such as pain, contractures, and hip displacement.

NICE (2019) provides detailed recommendations for care of adults with CP. They recommend consideration of regular reviews at agreed upon frequency and tailored to needs and preferences, and annual reviews by a healthcare professional with expertise in neurodisabilities for those with complex needs. Focus on the areas of function and participation (communication, vocational skills and independent living, electronic assistive technology, and physical activity). Interventions to consider are those addressing abnormal muscle tone (spasticity and dystonia), including addressing factors that can exacerbate this problem such as bladder and bowel problems, pain and pressure sores); monitoring and addressing clinical complications and comorbidities as discussed above; mental health problems; eating and nutritional problems; respiratory difficulties; and pain.

Ultrasound elastography may be useful for assessing muscle stiffness, monitoring its temporal changes, and measuring response to intervention if a more objective measure is needed beyond functional assessment.

Offer a hip X-ray if the patient reports hip pain, there is a clinically important leg-length discrepancy, increased hip muscle tone, deterioration in sitting or standing or increasing difficulty with perineal care or hygiene.

At the time of diagnosis, most patients are very young children, so the advice and guidance is for their caregivers. Because the diagnosis is often overwhelming and life-changing, caregivers need a good support network and lots of reassurance and understanding.

NICE (2017) offers information about prognosis for walking for children with CP. The more severe the physical or cognitive impairment the greater the possibility of difficulties with walking. If a child is unable to sit at age 2 years, it is unlikely that they will walk unaided by age 6 years.

School-age children will need to be placed on individual education plans, and parents should be advised to request an evaluation at the beginning of each school year to discuss their goals in terms of therapy and education with the school. (Laws may vary by state, but they should check with the education board in their area.)

Advise parents to educate themselves about the numerous government programs designed to protect their child's legal rights and programs to help with the extensive financial pressures they may face in having a child with CP.

Many women with CP are sexually active. In a longitudinal 4-year study of 103 young adults with CP who had a high level of physical function and no intellectual impairment, 60% reported having intercourse by year 4. Questions about sexuality and need for contraception should be asked and assistance provided.

There is very limited information regarding pregnancy in women with CP. In an interview study of 22 women with mobility impairment, 4 of whom had CP, impairment-related complications during pregnancy included falls; bladder and bowel problems; wheelchair fit and stability problems that compromised safety; shortness of breath, sometimes requiring respiratory support; increased spasticity; and skin integrity problems.

In a matched cohort study, the 34 women with physical disabilities who gave birth experienced higher rates of preterm birth, low-birth-weight infants, and pregnancy complications than their non-disabled counterparts.

In a systematic review of 23 studies, women with a disability (pooled unadjusted OR 1.45, 95% CI, 1.16-1.82) and intellectual and developmental disabilities (pooled unadjusted OR 1.77, 95% CI, 1.21-2.60) had increased risk for hypertensive disorders of pregnancy. In addition, women with any (pooled unadjusted OR 1.31, 95% CI 1.02-1.68), physical (pooled unadjusted OR 1.60, 95% CI, 1.21-2.13), and intellectual and developmental disabilities (pooled unadjusted OR 1.29, 95% CI, 1.02-1.63) also had increased risk for cesarean delivery.

In a national sample of women giving birth in England, disabled women, comprising 6.14% (1,482) of the total sample surveyed, reported higher rates of use of maternity services and were less likely to breastfeed than non-disabled women. Most were positive about their maternity care and reported sufficient access and involvement, although physically-disabled women reported less choice about labor and birth.

feature.caption: The Gross Motor Function Classification System: A Reliable and Valid Method to Classify Functional Abilities and Limitations of Children With Cerebral Palsy.
feature.feature_body:
Level Between 2nd and 4th Birthdays Between 6th and 12th Birthdays
I Children floor sit with both hands free to manipulate objects. Movements in and out of floor sitting and standing are performed without adult assistance. Children walk as the preferred method of mobility without the need for any assistive mobility device. Children walk indoors and outdoors, and climb stairs without limitations. Children perform gross motor skills including running and jumping, but speed, balance, and coordination are reduced.
II Children floor sit but may have difficulty with balance when both hands are free to manipulate objects. Movements in and out of sitting are performed without adult assistance. Children pull to stand on a stable surface. Children crawl on hands and knees with a reciprocal pattern, cruise holding onto furniture, and walk using an assistive mobility device as preferred methods of mobility. Children walk indoors and outdoors, and climb stairs holding onto a railing but experience limitations walking on uneven surfaces and inclines, and walking in crowds or confined spaces. Children have at best only minimal ability to perform gross motor skills such as running and jumping.
III Children maintain floor sitting often by "W-sitting" (sitting between flexed and internally rotated hips and knees) and may require adult assistance to assume sitting. Children creep on their stomach or crawl on hands and knees (often without reciprocal leg movements) as their primary methods of self-mobility. Children may pull to stand on a stable surface and cruise short distances. Children may walk short distances indoors using an assistive mobility device and adult assistance for steering and turning. Children walk indoors or outdoors on a level surface with an assistive mobility device. Children may climb stairs holding onto a railing. Depending on upper limb function, children propel a wheelchair manually or are transported when traveling for long distances or outdoors on uneven terrain.
IV Children floor sit when placed but are unable to maintain alignment and balance without use of their hands for support. Children frequently require adaptive equipment for sitting and standing. Self-mobility for short distances (within a room) is achieved through rolling, creeping on stomach, or crawling on hands and knees without reciprocal leg movement. Children may maintain levels of function achieved before age 6 or rely more on wheeled mobility at home, at school, and in the community. Children may achieve self-mobility using a power wheelchair.
V Physical impairments restrict voluntary control of movement and the ability to maintain antigravity head and trunk postures. All areas of motor function are limited. Functional limitations in sitting and standing are not fully compensated for through the use of adaptive equipment and assistive technology. At Level V, children have no means of independent mobility and are transported. Some children achieve self-mobility using a power wheelchair with extensive adaptations. Functional limitations in sitting and standing are not fully compensated for through the use of adaptive equipment and assistive technology.
